title: A jealous baby (1.7)
hookLine: he watches an infant turn pale with jealousy and sees sin's roots
tomorrow: why would a grown man cry for a queen in a poem?

lines: THE TODDLER AND THE NEW BABY.
cards: There's a kind of family video: a toddler sees the new baby on mom's lap and the meltdown begins. Funny on a phone. Now the odd part.

Augustine is writing a book addressed to God, about his own sins, and in the middle of it he stops to describe a baby in a nursery. Not himself; he admits he can't remember being that small. Someone else's baby.
Why would a confession to God need a stranger's infant? Because he thinks something important is already happening there, before the child can say a word.

teach.h: PALE, BITTER, AND PLENTY OF MILK.
teach.b: So yes: a baby who can't talk can already be jealous. Augustine says he saw it himself. One infant watches another nursing at the same breast and goes pale, staring, bitter, though there's plenty of milk for both.
He adds the parts parents will recognize: the greedy crying, the fury at grownups, even its own parents, for not doing what it wants.
Mothers and nurses, he says, claim to charm such tempers away with remedies of their own, and everyone puts up with it, because it passes with age. Then the line that solves the puzzle.

teach.h: WEAK LIMBS, NOT AN INNOCENT WILL.
teach.b: It's the weakness of a baby's limbs that is innocent, he says, not its will. The baby is harmless because it's small, not because it wants nothing. That's why the nursery belongs in a confession.

Augustine is tracing his own story back past memory and finding the same bent will there at the start. Catholic teaching calls that inheritance original sin, and counts envy among the capital sins. But listen to his tone.
No horror at babies, and no blame. He's looking into a nursery and finding himself. And there's mercy in it: if envy can show up before speech, it isn't a shameful secret only you picked up.
It starts early. That makes it easier to name, and worth bringing to God.

how: Catholics preparing for confession may examine their conscience for small, everyday envy, which the Church counts among the capital sins (CCC 1866).

o: an infant already pale with envy, before words
a newborn who cries because it's hungry
a small child copying a sibling's bad habit

p: pale and bitter at the other child
what is innocent, not the will
the Church's name for the inheritance

s: Augustine thought babies were wicked and blamed them
no horror and no blame: he says a baby's weak limbs are innocent, and he finds himself in the nursery.
Augustine remembered his own envy as a baby
he says he can't remember his infancy; he watched another child.
the jealous baby had plenty of milk to share
that's what makes the stare so telling: there was enough for both.

games.q: your four-year-old nephew hides a friend's new toy truck, though he has five of his own. using Augustine's nursery, what's the honest read?
o: it's early envy, real but small; name it kindly with him.
it's nothing; he's too little for it to mean anything.
it's a sign he'll grow up mean; get strict now.
games.why: Augustine takes the small envy seriously without horror or blame. it's harmless because the child is small, and it can be named early.

practice: On a scrap of paper, write the name of one small envy you've carried lately, the kind a child would recognize: someone else's praise, someone else's plate, someone else's ease.
Then look at the words the way Augustine looked into the nursery, honestly and without disgust, and sit with the paper in your hand. Catholics who pray can name it to God just as plainly.

wordCard.voice: A jealous baby. In book one, Augustine watches an infant go pale with envy at another child, and sees how early the will bends.

carryVoice: The line to keep: it starts early, so it can be named without shame. Rest well.

sources.ref: Catechism of the Catholic Church 396–409 (original sin); 1866 (capital sins)
